messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 28
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Teacher
- Trauma Type: Stalking
- Pcl5: 52

She is 28, a secondary school teacher, and when she first talks about what happened she does it with the same careful sequencing she uses in the classroom, as if putting events in order might make them feel less chaotic. At the start, she says, it seems almost too small to call trauma. A message appears after a school theatre night from a man she vaguely recognizes as an older brother of a former student. He thanks her for “looking after” his sister and says she has a beautiful voice. She does not reply. Then there is another message, and another, each one more familiar in tone. He comments on clothes she wore that day at work, on the coffee she bought from the café near school, on the book in her hand at the train station. That is when she feels the first cold drop of fear: he is not just messaging her, he is watching her.

At first she tries to be polite, then firm, then silent. She blocks one account and he appears from another. Flowers are left outside her flat with no note, which somehow frightens her more than if he had signed his name. A colleague mentions that a man has been waiting near the school gates, not approaching, just standing there longer than any parent would. She begins leaving by a side entrance and asking another teacher to walk her to the station. She tells herself she is overreacting, then hates herself for minimizing it when she knows she is changing her whole life around his presence.

The turning point comes on a wet Thursday in November. She leaves school after a parents’ evening, tired and carrying exercise books home to mark. The street is quiet, and when she hears footsteps behind her she already knows, before she turns, who it is. He says her name softly, as though they know each other. He tells her he only wants to talk, that she has been cruel to ignore him, that he knows she gets scared walking alone. She cannot later remember everything he says, only the feeling of her skin turning numb and her mind becoming strangely sharp and distant at the same time. She gets into a corner shop and asks the cashier to call the police. Afterward, even though he does not touch her, her body behaves as if something violent has happened. She shakes uncontrollably that night. She vomits in the bathroom while her partner rubs her back. When she closes her eyes she sees him stepping out of the dark, hears her name in his voice.

There are reports, screenshots, statements, a court order eventually. On paper, people tell her, the situation is being handled. But her nervous system does not seem to care about paperwork. In the months that follow, she sleeps lightly and wakes at every sound in the corridor outside her flat. If a car idles too long on the street below, she is at the window before she can stop herself. She starts checking the lock three and four times before bed, then taking photos of the locked door so she can look at them from under the duvet and reassure herself she has done it. She dreams that he is inside the classroom, sitting among her pupils, smiling while she teaches as if he belongs there.

At work she keeps going, because teaching is one of the few parts of her identity she feels he has not completely stolen. But the classroom changes for her. She used to love the noisy rush before first period, students crowding in with stories and excuses and misplaced homework. Now sudden movement at the door makes her heart slam hard enough to hurt. If someone knocks unexpectedly on the classroom window, she loses track of what she is saying. During fire drills she has to fight the urge to run. She starts scanning faces at pickup time, searching automatically for him in every father, uncle, older brother. She knows this is irrational and also feels it is the only thing keeping her safe.

Her partner becomes both comfort and witness. He offers to collect her from school, to answer unknown numbers, to come with her everywhere, and she is grateful but also ashamed of how much she needs it. Before this, she had thought of herself as capable, independent, the teacher who could settle a difficult class with one look. Now she second-guesses her own judgment constantly. She asks, “Did you hear that?” so often that sometimes she stops herself mid-sentence, embarrassed. They argue about small things that are not small things: why she needs the curtains closed before sunset, why she cannot enjoy dinner if seated near the window, why she goes silent when a stranger looks at her too long.

What troubles her most is how the fear keeps renewing itself. She understands intellectually that the stalking has stopped, that there have been no sightings for months. Still, her body does not live in the same timeline. On the train she chooses seats near other women and never by the door. She varies her route to school even when she is running late. She no longer posts photos online. If a student mentions being watched or followed, a flush rises from her chest to her face and she has to grip the desk to stay present.

She says she misses the ordinary version of herself. Not a happier self, exactly, but a freer one. The hardest part is that nothing in her life now looks dramatic from the outside. She is still teaching, still living with her partner, still answering emails and marking essays and reminding Year 9 to put their phones away. Yet beneath that surface she is braced, listening, measuring exits, waiting for the world to become unsafe again.
